claim: Caffeine is the most widely consumed stimulant in the world.
source: Caffeine is the most widely consumed stimulant in the world (Planning Committee for a Workshop on Potential Health Hazards Associated with Consumption of Caffeine in Food and Dietary Supplements, Food and Nutrition Board, Board on Health Sciences Policy, Institute of Medicine, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Planning Committee for a Workshop on Potential Health Hazards Associated with Consumption of Caffeine in Food and Dietary Supplements, Food and Nutrition Board, Board on Health Sciences Policy, Institute of Medicine, 2014

claim: Caffeine produces a vascular response in the endothelium, causing vasodilation.
source: Caffeine produces a vascular response in the endothelium, causing vasodilation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge without specific citation in this sentence

claim: The vascular endothelium is the innermost layer of arteries.
source: The vascular endothelium, the innermost layer of arteries, is involved in several important functions, including regulation of blood flow, angiogenesis, thrombosis, and coagulation (Hadi et al., 2005; Krüger-Genge et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hadi et al., 2005 and Krüger-Genge et al., 2019

claim: The vascular endothelium is involved in regulation of blood flow, angiogenesis, thrombosis, and coagulation.
source: The vascular endothelium, the innermost layer of arteries, is involved in several important functions, including regulation of blood flow, angiogenesis, thrombosis, and coagulation (Hadi et al., 2005; Krüger-Genge et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hadi et al., 2005 and Krüger-Genge et al., 2019

claim: Endothelial dysfunction occurs in diseases such as atherosclerosis and hypertension.
source: Endothelial dysfunction occurs in diseases such as atherosclerosis and hypertension (Xu et al., 2021), eventually leading to coronary artery disease (CAD) (Matsuzawa and Lerman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2021

claim: Endothelial dysfunction eventually leads to coronary artery disease (CAD).
source: Endothelial dysfunction occurs in diseases such as atherosclerosis and hypertension (Xu et al., 2021), eventually leading to coronary artery disease (CAD) (Matsuzawa and Lerman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matsuzawa and Lerman, 2014

claim: Multiple studies have investigated the role of caffeine in cardiovascular disease with conflicting results.
source: Multiple studies have investigated the role of caffeine in cardiovascular disease (CVD), and more broadly, vascular health in general, with conflicting results (Chieng et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2014; Turnbull et al., 2017) on the role of caffeine in CVD risk.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chieng et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2014; Turnbull et al., 2017

claim: Ding et al., 2014 meta-analyzed 36 studies and found no association between heavy coffee consumption and increased risk of CVD.
source: Ding et al., 2014 meta-analyzed 36 studies and found no association between heavy coffee consumption and increased risk of CVD (Ding et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2014

claim: Turnbull et al., 2017 observed that moderate caffeine consumption was not associated with an increased risk of CVD or other cardiovascular events such as heart failure.
source: Similarly, Turnbull et al., 2017 observed that moderate caffeine consumption was not associated with an increased risk of CVD or other cardiovascular events such as heart failure (Turnbull et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turnbull et al., 2017

claim: Multiple studies suggested that caffeine may be beneficial in reducing the risk of CAD.
source: Multiple studies suggested that caffeine may be beneficial in reducing the risk of CAD (Choi et al., 2015; Miranda et al., 2018; Voskoboinik et al., 2019), while others provided evidence that caffeine may reduce the risk of heart failure, but had no significant effect on the risk of coronary heart disease or CVD (Stevens et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Choi et al., 2015; Miranda et al., 2018; Voskoboinik et al., 2019

claim: Caffeine may reduce the risk of heart failure, but had no significant effect on the risk of coronary heart disease or CVD.
source: Multiple studies suggested that caffeine may be beneficial in reducing the risk of CAD (Choi et al., 2015; Miranda et al., 2018; Voskoboinik et al., 2019), while others provided evidence that caffeine may reduce the risk of heart failure, but had no significant effect on the risk of coronary heart disease or CVD (Stevens et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stevens et al., 2021

claim: Chieng et al., 2022 found that decaffeinated, ground, and instant coffee significantly decreased CVD risk and mortality.
source: Most recently, Chieng et al., 2022 found that decaffeinated, ground, and instant coffee significantly decreased CVD risk and mortality (Chieng et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chieng et al., 2022

claim: Caffeine can induce changes in gene regulation in endothelial cells.
source: This study identified response factor motifs for caffeine, defined as transcription factor motifs that are enriched in differentially accessible regions, and demonstrated that caffeine can induce changes in gene regulation in endothelial cells.
evidence: Refers to a previous study (Findley et al., 2019) that demonstrated this finding

claim: SNPs within caffeine response factor binding sites were enriched for artery expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) colocalized with CAD risk variants.
source: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within caffeine response factor binding sites were enriched for artery expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) colocalized with CAD risk variants (Findley et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Findley et al., 2019

claim: The study used BiT-STARR-Seq to measure allelic effects on gene regulation for over 43,000 genetic variants.
source: To investigate GxE for caffeine, we treated vascular endothelial cells with caffeine and used a massively parallel reporter assay to measure allelic effects on gene regulation for over 43,000 genetic variants.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental approach used in this study

claim: The study identified 665 variants with allelic effects on gene regulation.
source: We identified 665 variants with allelic effects on gene regulation and 6 variants that regulate the gene expression response to caffeine (GxE, false discovery rate [FDR] < 5%).
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a result from the BiT-STARR-Seq experiments

claim: The study identified 6 variants that regulate the gene expression response to caffeine (GxE, FDR < 5%).
source: We identified 665 variants with allelic effects on gene regulation and 6 variants that regulate the gene expression response to caffeine (GxE, false discovery rate [FDR] < 5%).
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a result from the BiT-STARR-Seq experiments

claim: The library contained 43,556 target regulatory regions each containing an SNP in the middle with a total length of 200 nucleotides.
source: We designed 43,556 target regulatory regions each containing an SNP in the middle and with a total length of 200 nucleotides.
evidence: Described in the BiT-STARR-Seq Library Design section of Materials and methods

claim: The study observed 772 significantly differentially active targets: 546 upregulated targets and 226 downregulated targets (FDR < 10%).
source: We observed 772 significantly differentially active targets: 546 upregulated targets and 226 downregulated targets (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1), showing that caffeine overall increases the activity of the regulatory elements.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from DESeq2 analysis and shown in Figure 2A

claim: Caffeine overall increases the activity of the regulatory elements.
source: We observed 772 significantly differentially active targets: 546 upregulated targets and 226 downregulated targets (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1), showing that caffeine overall increases the activity of the regulatory elements.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that more targets are upregulated (546) than downregulated (226) in response to caffeine

claim: The motif for ZNF423, one of the caffeine response factors, was enriched within the differentially active targets.
source: We found the motif for ZNF423, one of the caffeine response factors, was enriched within the differentially active targets.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis using JASPAR database

claim: The three most enriched motifs were NFATC1, NFATC4, and NFATC2.
source: The three most enriched motifs were NFATC1, NFATC4, and NFATC2.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis results

claim: The NFAT transcription factor family is known for their involvement in the Ca2+/NFAT pathway.
source: The NFAT transcription factor family is known for their involvement in the Ca2+/NFAT pathway.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about NFAT transcription factors

claim: The Ca2+/NFAT signaling pathway plays an important role in maintaining the homeostasis of vascular endothelial cells.
source: This signaling pathway plays an important role in maintaining the homeostasis of vascular endothelial cells (Wang et al., 2020) and contributes to the mediation of proliferation and migration (Johnson et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020

claim: The Ca2+/NFAT pathway contributes to the mediation of proliferation and migration.
source: This signaling pathway plays an important role in maintaining the homeostasis of vascular endothelial cells (Wang et al., 2020) and contributes to the mediation of proliferation and migration (Johnson et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2003 and Wang et al., 2020

claim: Improper signaling of the Ca2+/NFAT pathway can induce endothelial dysfunction.
source: Thus, improper signaling of the Ca2+/NFAT pathway can induce endothelial dysfunction (Garcia-Vaz et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: In diabetic mice, NFAT expression exacerbated atherosclerosis.
source: In diabetic mice, NFAT expression exacerbated atherosclerosis (Blanco et al., 2018; Zetterqvist et al., 2014) and increased foam cell formation (Du et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blanco et al., 2018 and Zetterqvist et al., 2014

claim: In diabetic mice, NFAT expression increased foam cell formation.
source: In diabetic mice, NFAT expression exacerbated atherosclerosis (Blanco et al., 2018; Zetterqvist et al., 2014) and increased foam cell formation (Du et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Du et al., 2021

claim: In human coronary artery smooth muscle cells, NFAT signaling mediates vascular calcification.
source: In human coronary artery smooth muscle cells, NFAT signaling mediates vascular calcification (Goettsch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goettsch et al., 2011

claim: 19 motifs were enriched for being within upregulated targets.
source: We observed 19 motifs enriched for being within upregulated targets (Figure 2C) and 23 motifs enriched for being within downregulated targets (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis and shown in Figure 2C

claim: 23 motifs were enriched for being within downregulated targets.
source: We observed 19 motifs enriched for being within upregulated targets (Figure 2C) and 23 motifs enriched for being within downregulated targets (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis and shown in Figure 2D

claim: The motif for SREBF2 is enriched for being within downregulated targets.
source: We also observed that the motif for SREBF2, also called SREBP2, is enriched for being within downregulated targets.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis

claim: In hepatocytes, caffeine is known to suppress SREBF2 activity, which reduces PCSK9 expression, and thus increases LDLR expression, which could be protective against CVD.
source: In hepatocytes, caffeine is known to suppress SREBF2 activity, which reduces PCSK9 expression, and thus increases LDLR expression, which could be protective against CVD (Lebeau et al., 2022).

claim: The motif for TEAD4 was identified as enriched for being within downregulated targets.
source: The motif for TEAD4 was also identified as enriched for being within downregulated targets.

claim: A CAD GWAS risk variant disrupts binding of TEAD4 in smooth muscle cells, causing lower expression of p16, which could potentially contribute to the risk identified at this locus.
source: Interestingly, a CAD GWAS risk variant disrupts binding of TEAD4 in smooth muscle cells, causing lower expression of p16, which could potentially contribute to the risk identified at this locus (Almontashiri et al., 2015).

claim: 689 SNP/direction pairs (corresponding to 665 SNPs) showed significant ASE out of 50,914 SNP/direction pairs (30,680 SNPs) tested (2.2%, FDR < 10%).
source: We observed 689 SNP/direction pairs (corresponding to 665 SNPs) with significant ASE out of 50,914 SNP/direction pairs (30,680 SNPs) tested (2.2%, FDR < 10%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by ASE analysis using QuASAR-MPRA and shown in Figure 3A

claim: Negative control sequences tend to have higher p-values than other sequences in the library.
source: Additionally, our library contained negative control sequences that were predicted to not have an allelic regulatory effect. These negative control sequences tend to have higher p-values than other sequences in our library, as predicted (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by ASE analysis results shown in Figure 3A

claim: Genetic variation within regulatory sequences within the library can modulate gene expression levels in vascular endothelial cells.
source: These results demonstrate that genetic variation within regulatory sequences within our library can modulate gene expression levels in vascular endothelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of significant ASE in 689 SNP/direction pairs

claim: 6 significant SNP/direction pairs (corresponding to 6 SNPs) out of 23,814 (15,927 SNPs) tested showed cASE (FDR < 5%).
source: When testing for cASE, we observed 6 significant SNP/direction pairs (corresponding to 6 SNPs) out of 23,814 (15,927 SNPs) tested (FDR < 5%) (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by cASE analysis using ΔAST method and shown in Figure 3B

claim: There is an enrichment for cASE targets containing caffeine response factors.
source: Additionally, we annotated which of these cASE targets contains a known caffeine response factor as defined in Findley et al., 2019, based on ATAC-seq data. There is an enrichment for these targets containing caffeine response factors, as expected (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by annotation analysis and shown in Figure 3B

claim: ASE variants were 2.4-fold enriched within open chromatin regions (p<2.2e-16).
source: ASE variants were 2.4-fold enriched within open chromatin regions (p<2.2e-16, Figure 3C, green), while a more moderate trend was observed for cASE (1.2-fold, p=0.088, Figure 3C, purple).

claim: A more moderate trend was observed for cASE (1.2-fold, p=0.088) enrichment in open chromatin regions.
source: ASE variants were 2.4-fold enriched within open chromatin regions (p<2.2e-16, Figure 3C, green), while a more moderate trend was observed for cASE (1.2-fold, p=0.088, Figure 3C, purple).
evidence: Supported by Fisher's exact test and shown in Figure 3C

claim: ASE variants were 1.38 times more likely to be artery eQTLs (p=0.01).

evidence: Supported by Fisher's exact test and shown in Figure 3C

claim: A more moderate trend was observed for cASE variants (1.2 times more likely to be artery eQTLs, p=0.26).
source: We observed a more moderate trend for cASE variants (1.2 times more likely to be artery eQTLs, p=0.26, Figure 3C, purple, Supplementary file 3).

claim: 44 motifs were enriched for targets containing ASE variants.

claim: NRF1 is enriched for targets containing cASE and ASE variants and is known to regulate lipid metabolism.

claim: KLF15 and KLF14 are enriched in targets with cASE and ASE.

claim: KLF14 has previously been associated with CVD.
source: KLF15 is involved in cardiac lipid metabolism (Prosdocimo et al., 2014; Prosdocimo et al., 2015), and KLF14 has previously been associated with CVD (Fryar et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2018).

claim: Genetic variation may modulate the response to caffeine by increasing binding activity of INSM1 and PLAG1 transcription factors.
source: Factors INSM1 and PLAG1 are caffeine response factors as defined in Findley et al., 2019, confirming that genetic variation may modulate the response to caffeine by increasing binding activity of these transcription factors.

claim: GABP is a known repressor of transcription.

claim: A caffeine concentration of 1.16 × 10–3 M was used for treatment.
source: We used a caffeine concentration of 1.16 × 10–3 M.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: Water was used as a vehicle control.
source: In addition, water was used as a vehicle control as that was the solvent used to prepare the caffeine treatment.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: The library of target regulatory sequences consisted of eQTLs, SNPs predicted to disrupt transcription factor binding (centiSNPs), and SNPs associated with complex traits in GWAS.
source: Briefly, the library of target regulatory sequences consisted of several categories of regulatory variants, including eQTLs (Innocenti et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2015), SNPs predicted to disrupt transcription factor binding (centiSNPs) (Moyerbrailean et al., 2016a), and SNPs associated with complex traits in GWAS (Pickrell, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citations

claim: Negative controls that were not predicted to have a regulatory effect were included in the library.
source: Negative controls that were not predicted to have a regulatory effect were also included in the library (Moyerbrailean et al., 2016a).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation

claim: The DNA library was transfected into HUVECs using the Lonza Nucleofector X platform.
source: The DNA library was transfected into HUVECs using the Lonza Nucleofector X platform.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: Cells were electroporated using the DS-120 setting with primary cell solution P5.
source: Cells were electroporated using the DS-120 setting with primary cell solution P5.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: Caffeine was added at 1.16 × 10–3 M after transfection.
source: Caffeine was added at 1.16 × 10–3 M after transfection.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: Cells were incubated for 24 hr and lysed.
source: Cells were incubated for 24 hr and lysed.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: 6 replicates per treatment condition (caffeine and the water vehicle control) or 12 replicates in total were completed.
source: We completed 6 replicates per treatment condition (caffeine and the water vehicle control) or 12 replicates in total.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: The average sequencing depth per library was 39,235,611 reads, for a total of 470,827,333 reads.
source: The average sequencing depth per library was 39,235,611 reads, for a total of 470,827,333 reads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: DESeq2 was used to test for a molecular response to caffeine.
source: To test for a molecular response to caffeine, we used the R package DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation

claim: The model tested the effect of treatment, correcting for allele (~allele + treatment).
source: Our model tested the effect of treatment, correcting for allele (~allele + treatment), as we observed a strong allelic effect.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: QuASAR-MPRA was used to test for ASE.
source: To test for ASE, we utilized the R package quantitative allele-specific analysis of reads (QuASAR-MPRA) (Kalita et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation

claim: QuASAR-MPRA uses a beta-binomial model and accounts for uneven initial allelic proportions present in the DNA library.
source: QuASAR-MPRA uses a beta-binomial model and accounts for uneven initial allelic proportions present in the DNA library.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: The ΔAST method was used to test for cASE.
source: To test for cASE, we used a method previously developed by our lab called differential allele-specific test, or ΔAST.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: The motif scan was completed using the PWMScan tool, using all PWMs within the JASPAR 2022 CORE database (838 motifs).
source: The motif scan was completed using the PWMScan tool, using all PWMs within the JASPAR (Castro-Mondragon et al., 2022) 2022 CORE database (838 motifs).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation

claim: DAP-G was used to fine-map eQTLs from all three artery tissues in GTEx V8.
source: These probabilities are then used in DAP-G (Zhang et al., 2020) to fine-map eQTLs from all three artery tissues in GTEx V8.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation

claim: A total of 364,427,888 eQTLs were fine-mapped across three artery tissues.
source: A total of 364,427,888 eQTLs were fine-mapped across three artery tissues.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section

claim: Colocalization analysis of the causal GWAS variants with eQTLs was performed using fastENLOC.
source: To better understand how cASE variants may impact traits related to cardiovascular health, we performed colocalization analysis of the causal GWAS variants with eQTLs using fastENLOC (Wen et al., 2017) by integration of fine-mapped eQTLs in the three artery tissues (see above section) and fine-mapped GWAS signals for CAD and hypertension.
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation

claim: The R package INTACT was used to estimate the probability of putative causal genes by combining evidence from colocalization and TWAS.
source: To overcome the limitations in a single approach, we combined the evidence from colocalization and TWAS to estimate the probability of putative causal genes using the R package INTACT (Okamoto et al., 2023).
evidence: Stated in the Materials and methods section with supporting citation
